articleSummary:

The ongoing outbreak is the largest in the country’s history and was officially declared on 15 May, with officials noting it likely began several weeks earlier. Ebola typically causes severe fever and can progress to bleeding, underscoring the seriousness of surveillance and response efforts. As of 28 September 2026, the outbreak has far exceeded the 2018–2020 event, which caused about 2,300 deaths and roughly 3,500 cases. The article does not provide details on infection source, cross-border links, or specific control measures.

The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus and stands as the largest and deadliest Ebola event in the DRC’s history, surpassing the 2018–2020 epidemic. It ranks as the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record after the 2014–2016 West Africa epidemic, which infected more than 28,600 people and killed over 11,000 in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone. The figures underscore the severity of the ongoing crisis within the DRC and highlight the enduring transmission threat in the region.

articleSummary: One month after a massive landslide along the Nepal–China border that killed about 1,500 and left more than 5,200 missing, a Japanese Red Cross nurse reported rising infectious disease risks from the disaster. Nurse Sachiko Kawase of Osaka Red Cross Hospital, who arrived Sept 7, described in an online Sept 24 press conference how community disruption is complicating health needs. Chronic conditions such as diabetes require continuity of care, with some patients being transferred to other cities to manage complications. Infectious disease outbreaks are a critical concern; cholera persists in the area and diarrheal illnesses could spread amid crowded shelters, unsafe water and limited sanitation. Humanitarian efforts focus on dignified shelter, provision of toilets and water, and mental health support. Kawase will remain through Oct 9 to continue planning and coordination with Nepal Red Cross and local authorities.

articleHeadline: Food poisoning outbreak at an internationally renowned Macau hotel; eight people across two groups affected; lobster and scallops suspected as the source.
articleSummary: As of 28 September 2026, eight people across two dining groups developed fever, abdominal pain, and diarrhea after dining at The Parisian Macao buffet along the Cotai Strip, Macau. The Macau Health Bureau and the Civic and Municipal Affairs Bureau's Food Safety Office reported the case cluster and launched epidemiological investigations. The restaurant was ordered to immediately halt sale of implicated items, conduct thorough cleaning and disinfection, and collect food and environmental samples for laboratory testing to identify the pathogen. Preliminary findings point to a bacterial cause, with Vibrio parahaemolyticus highlighted as a likely culprit given high-risk seafood and multi-step dishes such as cheese-baked lobster, steamed scallops, and abalone tart. Salmonella and Staphylococcus aureus are also considered. The self-service buffet setup is noted for potential cross-contamination and temperature abuse; public health guidance emphasizes hot foods above 60°C, cold foods below 4°C, separate serving utensils, hand hygiene, and caution for high-risk groups.

articleHeadline: Outbreak alert on a tourist island: Hundreds of people were hospitalized.
articleSummary: An ongoing gastroenteritis outbreak on Rhodes Island, Greece, since July 2026 has led to hundreds of hospitalizations. Data reported by Greek state television (ERT) indicate the illness accounts for about one-third of emergency department visits at Rhodes Hospitals. The surge peaked in August, with Rhodes Hospital averaging about 40 gastroenteritis presentations daily; by September the daily rate had declined to around 30. Laboratory investigations have ruled out water supply or sewage as the source, pinpointing a highly transmissible virus spread through close contact and food. Symptoms described as stomach and intestinal infection, typical of viral gastroenteritis, are driving rapid in-hospital comings and intense patient load. The outbreak underscores the risk to the popular tourist destination during the peak summer season and ongoing transmission into early autumn 2026.

articleHeadline: Leprosy
articleSummary: Leprosy (Hansen’s disease) remains a public health issue in the Philippines, though elimination occurred in 1998. A pediatric perspective notes ongoing transmission; DOH 2020–2024 data show most new cases in adults 20–59 and persistent cases in children 0–14. WHO 2024 data indicate a Southeast Asia–wide burden. Mycobacterium leprae transmits mainly via respiratory droplets; incubation is 2–5 years; close contact is required and it is less contagious than measles or influenza. Presentation may include facial/ear involvement with lion-like facies, thickened features, loss of eyebrows/eyelashes, nodular lesions, and nasal bridge flattening; hands/feet can develop claw deformities or hypopigmented plaques; hypoesthesia is a red flag. Diagnosis is clinical, with skin-slit smear or punch biopsy. MDT is free for 6–12 months; rifampicin reduces transmission; BCG offers 20–80% protection; patients become noncontagious within 1–2 weeks. In the case, a child also had tuberculosis, underscoring the need for strengthened national programs.
notes: 1998年に排除認定済みのハンセン病について、小児科的視点からの啓発・教育的オピニオン記事。既知の疾患の慢性的状況説明であり、新規アウトブレイクではない。

articleHeadline: Regular preventive care keeps dogs safe from leptospirosis
articleSummary: Leptospirosis remains a significant risk for dogs in the Philippines during the rainy season, with floodwaters and puddles in Manila and other urban areas potentially contaminated by rats' urine. Dogs acquire leptospirosis through contact with contaminated water, soil, or environments, and early signs include fever, lethargy, vomiting, and diarrhea; severe infections can damage kidneys and liver, cause bleeding, and lead to serious complications. Preventive care is emphasized year-round: keep vaccinations up to date, maintain parasite protection, avoid exposure to puddles and floodwater, provide clean drinking water, reduce rodent access, and schedule regular veterinary visits for early detection. The warning comes as August’s Habagat rains give way to El Niño, which may affect the southern Philippines later this year. Dr. Vincent Casimero of Boehringer Ingelheim Philippines underscores that protecting dogs helps protect families and communities.

articleSummary: African Swine Fever (ASF) cases in Tabuk City, Kalinga, prompt urgent reporting of suspected infections. Surveillance covers 18 of 43 barangays, with Agbannawag, Nambaran, Malalao, Bulo, Bulanao, Calanan, New Ganglag, Gobgob, Masablang, San Juan, Casigayan, Dilag, Laya West, Appas, and Cudal among affected areas; Cabaruan has been removed after five months with no new cases. articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) nears 8,000 confirmed cases, with 7,911 cases and 3,801 deaths (case-fatality ~48%).
